Exercise 5.1: Goldilocks and the step size



Consider f(x_1, x_2) = x_1^2/2 + 25\,x_2^2/2, with gradient \nabla f = (x_1, \, 25 x_2), starting point (-8, 2), and true minimum (0,0).

Using the stability condition \gamma < 2/\lambda_{\max}, predict the largest stable step size. Check your prediction by running grad_descent() with \gamma just below and just above it (a small n, say 100, is enough to see divergence).
Use steps_to_tol() to count the iterations needed to get within 10^{-3} of the minimum for \gamma = 0.005, 0.04 and 0.07 (use a generous n, e.g. 20000). What do you conclude about how to choose \gamma?






5.1.2 Estimation is optimisation
So far f has been a toy. Here is why statisticians care. A huge share of estimators are defined as the minimiser of an average loss over the data:

\hat{\theta} = \arg\min_{\theta} L(\theta),
\qquad
L(\theta) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell_i(\theta),

where \ell_i(\theta) measures how badly the parameter \theta explains observation i. You have met one member of this family already: least squares, with \ell_i(\boldsymbol\beta) = \tfrac{1}{2}(y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^\top \boldsymbol\beta)^2 and gradient \nabla L(\boldsymbol\beta) = \tfrac{1}{n} X^\top (X\boldsymbol\beta - \mathbf{y}). Least squares is also the family’s great exception: setting its gradient to zero gives the normal equations X^\top X \boldsymbol\beta = X^\top \mathbf{y}, a linear system that solve() (np.linalg.solve() in Python) dispatches in one line, with no iteration in sight. That is exactly the magic formula \hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y} you used in Challenge 1.1 of Chapter 1, and the reason this chapter spends no more time on it. Almost no other model is so lucky. Our running example is the everyday kind, where no closed form exists and iterating is the only way down.
Logistic regression (negative log-likelihood). For binary y_i \in \{0, 1\} the model is \Pr(y_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = \sigma(\eta_i), where \eta_i = \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta is the linear predictor (the code below calls it eta) and \sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z}) is the sigmoid function, which squashes the real line into (0, 1) so that \eta_i, which can be any real number, becomes a probability. Taking -\log of the likelihood and averaging over the observations gives the loss; differentiating the loss gives the gradient:

L(\boldsymbol\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
  \Big[ \log\!\big(1 + e^{\mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}\big)
        - y_i \, \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta \Big],
\qquad
\nabla L(\boldsymbol\beta) = \frac{1}{n} X^\top\big(\sigma(X\boldsymbol\beta) - \mathbf{y}\big),

with the rows \mathbf{x}_i^\top stacked into the design matrix X and \sigma applied elementwise. These two formulas are all the code will need. The gradient is worth reading aloud once: observation i contributes \nabla \ell_i(\boldsymbol\beta) = \big(\sigma(\eta_i) - y_i\big)\,\mathbf{x}_i, predicted probability minus observed outcome (a residual on the probability scale) times its own covariates, so observations the model already gets right contribute almost nothing while confidently wrong ones push hard; this per-observation piece is also exactly the single-sample gradient that SGD will draw at random in Section 5.1.3. Note how the least-squares gradient at the top of this section, \tfrac{1}{n} X^\top(X\boldsymbol\beta - \mathbf{y}), has the same shape: both say “X^\top times (prediction minus data)”, the fingerprint of the generalised linear model family that R’s glm() is named after. Tidy as the gradient is, setting it to zero gives equations with no closed-form solution: you must optimise numerically. This is the everyday reality of maximum likelihood.
If you’re wondering where the two formulas come from, the proof below is optional. It is worth reading once in your life, though, in particular if you are planning to continue with your studies. This derivation you will redo, with a different likelihood each time, for every model you ever fit by maximum likelihood.






[OPTIONAL] Proof: from likelihood to loss to gradient





Step 1 We write down the negative log-likelihood. Observation i is a Bernoulli trial with success probability p_i = \sigma(\eta_i), so its probability mass is p_i^{y_i} (1 - p_i)^{1 - y_i} (check it: this equals p_i when y_i = 1 and 1 - p_i when y_i = 0). Independence multiplies the contributions, -\log turns the product into a sum, and dividing by n gives the average-loss form:

L(\boldsymbol\beta)
= -\frac{1}{n} \log \prod_{i=1}^n p_i^{y_i} (1 - p_i)^{1 - y_i}
= -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n
  \Big[ y_i \log p_i + (1 - y_i) \log(1 - p_i) \Big].

The parameters hide inside p_i = \sigma(\eta_i), so before differentiating we rewrite everything in terms of \eta_i. Multiplying the top and bottom of \sigma(\eta) = 1/(1 + e^{-\eta}) by e^{\eta} gives \sigma(\eta) = e^{\eta}/(1 + e^{\eta}), hence 1 - \sigma(\eta) = 1/(1 + e^{\eta}), and taking logs:

\log \sigma(\eta) = \eta - \log\big(1 + e^{\eta}\big),
\qquad
\log\big(1 - \sigma(\eta)\big) = -\log\big(1 + e^{\eta}\big).

Substituting both into the i-th summand \ell_i of L:

\ell_i(\boldsymbol\beta)
= -y_i \big[ \eta_i - \log\big(1 + e^{\eta_i}\big) \big]
  + (1 - y_i) \log\big(1 + e^{\eta_i}\big)
= \log\big(1 + e^{\eta_i}\big) - y_i \, \eta_i,

the two logarithm terms merging because their coefficients y_i and 1 - y_i sum to one. Averaging the \ell_i:

L(\boldsymbol\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
  \Big[ \log\!\big(1 + e^{\mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}\big)
        - y_i \, \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta \Big].

Step 2. We differentiate, by first noting that the derivative of \log(1 + e^{\eta}) (machine learning people call this function the softplus), is the sigmoid again:

\frac{d}{d\eta} \log\big(1 + e^{\eta}\big)
= \frac{e^{\eta}}{1 + e^{\eta}}
= \sigma(\eta).

Second, we note that \eta_i = \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta is linear in \boldsymbol\beta with \nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}\, \eta_i = \mathbf{x}_i, so a term g(\eta_i) contributes g'(\eta_i)\, \mathbf{x}_i to the gradient. Applying both to \ell_i = \log(1 + e^{\eta_i}) - y_i \eta_i:

\nabla \ell_i(\boldsymbol\beta)
= \sigma(\eta_i)\, \mathbf{x}_i - y_i\, \mathbf{x}_i
= \big(\sigma(\eta_i) - y_i\big)\, \mathbf{x}_i .

Averaging over the sample and stacking the rows \mathbf{x}_i^\top into the design matrix X packs the sum into one matrix product:

\nabla L(\boldsymbol\beta)
= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \big(\sigma(\eta_i) - y_i\big)\, \mathbf{x}_i
= \frac{1}{n} X^\top\big(\sigma(X\boldsymbol\beta) - \mathbf{y}\big),

with \sigma applied elementwise: exactly the two formulas claimed above. \square



Example. Let us simulate a dataset to fit. We fix the random seed first (set.seed() in R, a seeded generator np.random.default_rng() in Python) so that you get the same data, plots and fitted values as these notes.
Note: Remember that the two languages cannot share a random stream, so we will get slightly different results.


R

set.seed(7432)

# --- logistic regression data: intercept + one covariate --------------------
n_log <- 500
x_log <- rnorm(n_log)
X_log <- cbind(1, x_log)                  # design matrix: intercept + slope
beta_log_true <- c(-0.5, 2)
p_true <- 1 / (1 + exp(-as.vector(X_log %*% beta_log_true)))
y_log <- rbinom(n_log, 1, p_true)

sigmoid <- \(z) 1 / (1 + exp(-z))
nll <- \(b) {
  eta <- as.vector(X_log %*% b)
  mean(log(1 + exp(eta)) - y_log * eta)
}
nll_grad <- \(b) {
  p <- sigmoid(as.vector(X_log %*% b))
  as.vector(t(X_log) %*% (p - y_log)) / n_log
}

rng = np.random.default_rng(7432)

# --- logistic regression data: intercept + one covariate --------------------
n_log = 500
x_log = rng.normal(size=n_log)
X_log = np.column_stack([np.ones(n_log), x_log])   # design matrix: intercept + slope
beta_log_true = np.array([-0.5, 2])
p_true = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X_log @ beta_log_true)))
y_log = rng.binomial(1, p_true)

sigmoid = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
def nll(b):
    eta = X_log @ b
    return np.mean(np.log(1 + np.exp(eta)) - y_log * eta)

def nll_grad(b):
    p = sigmoid(X_log @ b)
    return X_log.T @ (p - y_log) / n_log



Time to descend. The model has two parameters, so we can watch gradient descent walk over the loss surface of a real statistical model exactly as we watched it cross the toy bowls. We start from \boldsymbol\beta = (0, 0), which predicts every observation as a 50/50 coin toss, and take a hand-tuned \gamma = 2: large, but safe here, because the contours below reveal a friendly, nearly round bowl (small \kappa). Exercise 5.3 shows how quickly that luxury disappears on real covariates.


R

path_nll <- grad_descent(nll_grad, x0 = c(0, 0), gamma = 2, n = 200)

beta_hat <- unlist(tail(path_nll, 1)[1:2])   # the final iterate

Note also that beta_hat lands near the true (-0.5, 2) that generated the data but not on it: the gap is the sampling error of maximum likelihood, not a failure of the optimiser, and running more iterations would not shrink it.

x1, x2, f_grid = contour_data(nll, (-1.2, 0.6), (-0.4, 2.4))
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.contour(x1, x2, f_grid, levels=20, colors="0.7", linewidths=0.5)

The contours are contours of the NLL L(\beta_0, \beta_1): a picture worth keeping in mind every time you fit any model. The path marches straight into the bowl and stops at the maximum likelihood estimate. The fit itself is done; what the rest of the chapter adds is how to get there cheaply when n is enormous (Section 5.1.3), and how to stop hand-tuning \gamma (Section 5.2.2).

5.1.2.1 Approximate gradients
What if we cannot compute the gradient? Perhaps the loss is a black box written by someone else, or the likelihood is a page of algebra we would rather not differentiate. The descent seems stuck before it starts, but remember what a partial derivative is: the limit of a difference quotient. We can simply stop short of the limit. For a small h, each partial derivative is well approximated by its central difference:

\frac{\partial L}{\partial \beta_j}(\boldsymbol\beta)
\;\approx\;
\frac{L(\boldsymbol\beta + h\, \mathbf{e}_j) - L(\boldsymbol\beta - h\, \mathbf{e}_j)}{2h},

where \mathbf{e}_j has a one in position j and zeros elsewhere. A loop over the coordinates (Chapter 2) wrapped in a function that takes f as an argument (Chapter 3) turns the definition into code. How close does it get? Since here we do know the exact gradient, we can measure the approximation error directly:


R

# approximate each partial derivative of f by a central difference
num_grad <- function(f, b, h = 1e-6) {
  g <- numeric(length(b))
  for (j in seq_along(b)) {
    e <- numeric(length(b))
    e[j] <- h
    g[j] <- (f(b + e) - f(b - e)) / (2 * h)
  }
  g
}

b_test <- c(0.5, -1)
num_grad(nll, b_test) - nll_grad(b_test)   # approximation error at a test point

[1] -2.808398e-11 -7.505441e-12




Python

# approximate each partial derivative of f by a central difference
def num_grad(f, b, h=1e-6):
    g = np.zeros(len(b))
    for j in range(len(b)):
        e = np.zeros(len(b))
        e[j] = h
        g[j] = (f(b + e) - f(b - e)) / (2 * h)
    return g

b_test = np.array([0.5, -1])
num_grad(nll, b_test) - nll_grad(b_test)   # approximation error at a test point

array([-5.39799039e-11,  4.99606467e-11])




An error of order 10^{-11}: for all practical purposes, num_grad recovers the gradient without a single line of calculus. (Note that the same comparison, run in reverse, is a debugging tool: whenever you have derived a gradient by hand, it is always possible to check it against a numerical counterpart)
To descend with the approximate gradient, notice that grad_descent() never looks inside its grad argument; any function that maps a vector to a vector will do, including one manufactured on the spot from the loss itself. That is a job for a function factory (Section 3.5.2): curry the loss L and the step h into num_grad, receive a function of \boldsymbol\beta alone, and hand that straight to grad_descent(). As an example, we rerun the descent and compare with the exact-gradient run:


R

# factory: fix f and h once, get back a gradient function of b alone
make_num_grad <- function(f, h = 1e-6) \(b) num_grad(f, b, h)

path_num <- grad_descent(make_num_grad(nll), x0 = c(0, 0), gamma = 2, n = 200)

c(steps_exact = steps_to_tol(path_nll, beta_hat),
  steps_num   = steps_to_tol(path_num, beta_hat))

steps_exact   steps_num

rbind(exact     = beta_hat,
      numerical = unlist(tail(path_num, 1)[1:2]))

exact     -0.5081276 1.823676
numerical -0.5081276 1.823676

# factory: fix f and h once, get back a gradient function of b alone
def make_num_grad(f, h=1e-6):
    return lambda b: num_grad(f, b, h)

path_num = grad_descent(make_num_grad(nll), x0=np.array([0.0, 0.0]), gamma=2, n=200)

{"steps_exact": steps_to_tol(path_nll, beta_hat),

{'steps_exact': 50, 'steps_num': 50}

pd.DataFrame([beta_hat, path_num.iloc[-1, :2].to_numpy()],
             index=["exact", "numerical"])

                  0         1
exact     -0.638074  1.891555
numerical -0.638074  1.891555




Same number of steps into a 10^{-3} ball around beta_hat, the same estimate to the printed precision (the true gap is about 10^{-10}), and we never differentiated anything. The price is in the operation count: each step now costs 2d evaluations of the full loss (here 4 \times 200 = 800 passes over the data, against 200 for the exact gradient), a bill that grows with the dimension; and the finite-difference error, harmless here, can bite on badly scaled problems. This trick is exactly what optim() and minimize() quietly do whenever you call them without supplying a gradient. It is also half of a bigger idea: if first derivatives can be built from differences of the loss, then curvature can be built from differences of gradients. That observation powers BFGS, the workhorse of the next section.



5.1.3 Stochastic gradient descent
Look again at the gradient of the average loss:

\nabla L(\theta) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \nabla \ell_i(\theta).

Every single step of gradient descent touches all n observations. For our n = 500 example that is nothing; for n = 10^8 user records it means one step of GD costs a full pass over a dataset that may not even fit in memory. The sum structure suggests a bold shortcut: don’t compute the whole sum. Pick one index I uniformly at random and use \nabla \ell_I(\theta) as a stand-in for \nabla L(\theta). It is a noisy stand-in, but it is unbiased: \mathbb{E}\big[\nabla \ell_I(\theta)\big] = \nabla L(\theta). On average, it is the right direction. The update

\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \gamma_t \, \nabla \ell_{I_t}(\theta_t),
\qquad I_t \sim \text{Uniform}\{1, \dots, n\},

is stochastic gradient descent (SGD). The step size has quietly acquired a subscript t, and it is load-bearing. With the full gradient, the steps shrink on their own as the minimum approaches, because \nabla L \to \mathbf{0} there. The noisy stand-in does us no such favour: even standing exactly at the minimiser, a randomly drawn observation pushes the iterate somewhere (only the average of the pushes is zero), so with a constant \gamma the iterates can never settle. They reach the neighbourhood of the minimiser quickly and then rattle around it forever, in a “noise ball” whose radius grows with \gamma. The cure is a decaying schedule \gamma_t: shrink the steps to damp the noise, but not so fast that the algorithm runs out of fuel before arriving. The classical recipe (Robbins and Monro, 1951: this algorithm is older than the computer you are running it on) asks, informally, for

\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \gamma_t = \infty
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \gamma_t^2 < \infty:

infinite total travel, so the iterate can reach the minimiser however far away it started, but finite total squared steps, so the noise averages out. Schedules like \gamma_t = a/(b + t) satisfy both, which is why you keep seeing that shape.
A compromise between one sample and all n is a mini-batch: average \nabla\ell_i over a random subset B of size m. Still unbiased, with variance shrinking like 1/m, at cost proportional to m. The economics are the whole point:

one GD step costs O(n) per-observation gradients;
one SGD step costs O(1) (or O(m) for a mini-batch), regardless of n.

When n is huge, SGD has taken thousands of noisy-but-useful steps before GD finishes its first.
Algorithm 5.2 states the mini-batch recipe precisely, with single-sample SGD as the special case m = 1.






Algorithm 5.2: Stochastic gradient descent (mini-batch)



Input: objective L(\theta) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell_i(\theta) with per-observation gradients \nabla \ell_i, start point \theta_0, step sizes \gamma_t > 0 (constant, or decaying like \gamma_t = a/(b + t)), batch size m, number of steps n_{\text{steps}}.
Output: the trajectory \theta_0, \theta_1, \dots, \theta_{n_{\text{steps}}}.

for t = 1, 2, \dots, n_{\text{steps}}:

draw a subset B_t \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\} of size m, uniformly at random, without replacement
\theta_t \leftarrow \theta_{t-1} - \gamma_t \, \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i \in B_t} \nabla \ell_i(\theta_{t-1})

return \theta_0, \theta_1, \dots, \theta_{n_{\text{steps}}}

Single-sample SGD is the case m = 1: step (a) draws one index I_t \sim \text{Uniform}\{1, \dots, n\} and step (b) becomes the update displayed above, \theta_t \leftarrow \theta_{t-1} - \gamma_t \, \nabla \ell_{I_t}(\theta_{t-1}). Note the index base: the step that produces \theta_t uses \gamma_t, which is exactly the code’s gamma(t), so the first update uses \gamma_1.


Here is single-sample SGD in the same functional style. The step size enters as a function of the step number t, so that constant and decaying schedules fit the same interface, and the per-observation gradient grad_i we feed it is an old friend: exactly the (\sigma(\eta_i) - y_i)\,\mathbf{x}_i derived in Section 5.1.2.


R

sgd <- function(grad_i, x0, gamma, n_steps, n_data) {
  # grad_i(theta, i): gradient of the loss at observation i only
  # gamma(t): step size at step t
  path <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_steps + 1, ncol = length(x0))
  path[1, ] <- x0
  for (t in 1:n_steps) {
    i <- sample(n_data, 1)
    path[t + 1, ] <- path[t, ] - gamma(t) * grad_i(path[t, ], i)
  }
  out <- as.data.frame(path)
  names(out) <- paste0("x", seq_along(x0))
  out$iter <- 0:n_steps
  out
}

# single-observation gradient of the NLL: (sigmoid(eta_i) - y_i) * x_i
nll_grad_i <- function(b, i) X_log[i, ] * (sigmoid(sum(X_log[i, ] * b)) - y_log[i])



Python

def sgd(grad_i, x0, gamma, n_steps, n_data):
    # grad_i(theta, i): gradient of the loss at observation i only
    # gamma(t): step size at step t
    path = np.full((n_steps + 1, len(x0)), np.nan)
    path[0] = x0
    for t in range(1, n_steps + 1):
        i = rng.integers(n_data)
        path[t] = path[t - 1] - gamma(t) * grad_i(path[t - 1], i)
    out = pd.DataFrame(path, columns=[f"x{j + 1}" for j in range(len(x0))])
    out["iter"] = range(n_steps + 1)
    return out

# single-observation gradient of the NLL: (sigmoid(eta_i) - y_i) * x_i
nll_grad_i = lambda b, i: X_log[i] * (sigmoid(X_log[i] @ b) - y_log[i])



Note for Python: sample(n_data, 1) draws from \{1, \dots, n\}; rng.integers(n_data) draws from \{0, \dots, n-1\}: each exactly the right range for its language’s indexing. And where R’s sample() quietly uses the global RNG state, the Python column leans on the global rng object in the same way.
Let us run it on the logistic loss twice: once with a constant step size, once with a decaying one.


R

set.seed(1)
sgd_const <- sgd(nll_grad_i, c(0, 0), gamma = \(t) 0.2,           n_steps = 2000, n_data = n_log)
sgd_decay <- sgd(nll_grad_i, c(0, 0), gamma = \(t) 10 / (20 + t), n_steps = 2000, n_data = n_log)

sgd_const$schedule <- "constant: gamma_t = 0.2"
sgd_decay$schedule <- "decaying: gamma_t = 10/(20 + t)"
sgd_both <- rbind(sgd_const, sgd_decay)

# the cross marks beta_hat, the minimiser gradient descent found above
mle_pt <- data.frame(x1 = beta_hat[1], x2 = beta_hat[2])

ggplot(contour_data(nll, c(-1.6, 0.7), c(-0.5, 2.9)), aes(x1, x2)) +
  geom_contour(aes(z = f), bins = 20, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_path(data = sgd_both, colour = "#009E73", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(data = mle_pt, shape = 4, size = 3, colour = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ schedule) +
  labs(x = expression(beta[0]), y = expression(beta[1])) +
  theme_minimal()










Python

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
sgd_const = sgd(nll_grad_i, np.array([0.0, 0.0]), gamma=lambda t: 0.2,           n_steps=2000, n_data=n_log)
sgd_decay = sgd(nll_grad_i, np.array([0.0, 0.0]), gamma=lambda t: 10 / (20 + t), n_steps=2000, n_data=n_log)

# one subplot per schedule, same contours in each;
# the cross marks beta_hat, the minimiser gradient descent found above
titles = ["constant: gamma_t = 0.2", "decaying: gamma_t = 10/(20 + t)"]
x1, x2, f_grid = contour_data(nll, (-1.6, 0.7), (-0.5, 2.9))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.8), sharey=True)
for ax, p, ttl in zip(axes, [sgd_const, sgd_decay], titles):
    ax.contour(x1, x2, f_grid, levels=20, colors="0.7", linewidths=0.5)
    ax.plot(p["x1"], p["x2"], color="#009E73", linewidth=0.8)
    ax.scatter([beta_hat[0]], [beta_hat[1]], marker="x", s=60, color="black")
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$\beta_0$")
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$\beta_1$")
plt.show()










Both trajectories are noisy versions of the gradient descent path: that is the noise of estimating the gradient from one observation. And the endgames play out exactly as the theory promised: the constant step reaches the neighbourhood of \hat{\boldsymbol\beta} quickly and then rattles around it forever in its noise ball, while the decaying step still moves fast early on and then funnels into the minimum as the shrinking \gamma_t damps the noise.
Finally, the claim that actually sells SGD: progress per data point touched. One GD step costs n = 500 observation-gradients; one SGD step costs 1. Plot the loss against that budget:


R

sgd_decay$loss <- apply(as.matrix(sgd_decay[, 1:2]), 1, nll)

cost_df <- bind_rows(
  tibble(evals = path_nll$iter * n_log, loss = path_nll$loss,  method = "GD (full gradient)"),
  tibble(evals = sgd_decay$iter,        loss = sgd_decay$loss, method = "SGD (one sample)")
) |>
  filter(evals > 0)

ggplot(cost_df, aes(evals, loss, colour = method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("GD (full gradient)" = "#0072B2",
                                 "SGD (one sample)" = "#009E73")) +
  labs(x = "observation-gradients computed (log scale)", y = "loss L") +
  theme_minimal()

                  "method": "SGD (one sample)"})
])

(ggplot(cost_df, aes("evals", "loss", colour="method"))
 + geom_line(size=0.7)
 + scale_x_log10()

                               "SGD (one sample)": "#009E73"})
 + labs(x="observation-gradients computed (log scale)", y="loss L")

Note for Python: pandas has no bind_rows() or filter() verbs; pd.concat() plus a boolean mask do the same job (Chapter 4). And plotnine still calls the line-width aesthetic size, which ggplot2 has since renamed linewidth.
By the time GD has finished its first step (500 evaluations), SGD has already collapsed most of the loss. Read the other end honestly too: GD then converges to the exact minimiser, while SGD closes in more slowly and less precisely. For small n and high accuracy, GD (or better, Section 5.2.2) wins; for enormous n and statistical-scale accuracy (remember the estimate itself has sampling error of order 1/\sqrt{n}, so chasing the tenth decimal of the minimiser is vanity), SGD is the only affordable option. It is the workhorse that trains essentially every neural network.

5.2 Fixing the geometry: preconditioning and BFGS
Back to the zig-zag valley of Section 5.1.1. The step size was capped by the steep direction, progress was throttled along the flat one, and the trajectory wasted its energy bouncing between walls. This section solves that geometry problem twice: first by hand, then automatically.

5.2.1 Preconditioning
If the valley is ten times steeper in x_2 than in x_1, then take steps ten times smaller in x_2. Formally, pick a symmetric positive-definite matrix P and update

\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = \mathbf{x}_t - \gamma \, P \, \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_t).

P reshapes the descent direction, stretching it in flat directions and shrinking it in steep ones. Plain gradient descent is P = I.
Algorithm 5.3 is Algorithm 5.1 with one matrix slipped in.






Algorithm 5.3: Preconditioned gradient descent



Input: objective f, gradient \nabla f, start point \mathbf{x}_0, step size \gamma > 0, a symmetric positive-definite matrix P, number of steps n_{\text{steps}} (the code’s n).
Output: the trajectory \mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_{n_{\text{steps}}}.

for t = 1, 2, \dots, n_{\text{steps}}:

\mathbf{x}_t \leftarrow \mathbf{x}_{t-1} - \gamma \, P \, \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_{t-1})

return \mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_{n_{\text{steps}}}

P = I recovers Algorithm 5.1. Taking P = (\nabla^2 f)^{-1}, the inverse Hessian recomputed at every iterate, with \gamma = 1, is Newton’s method (of which more shortly).




R

grad_descent_pre <- function(grad, x0, gamma, n, P) {
  path <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n + 1, ncol = length(x0))
  path[1, ] <- x0
  for (i in 1:n) {
    path[i + 1, ] <- path[i, ] - gamma * as.vector(P %*% grad(path[i, ]))
  }
  out <- as.data.frame(path)
  names(out) <- paste0("x", seq_along(x0))
  out$iter <- 0:n
  out
}



Python

def grad_descent_pre(grad, x0, gamma, n, P):
    path = np.full((n + 1, len(x0)), np.nan)
    path[0] = x0
    for i in range(n):
        path[i + 1] = path[i] - gamma * (P @ grad(path[i]))
    out = pd.DataFrame(path, columns=[f"x{j + 1}" for j in range(len(x0))])
    out["iter"] = range(n + 1)
    return out



What is the ideal P? Our valley has Hessian H = \mathrm{diag}(1, 10): curvature 1 along x_1, 10 along x_2. Choosing P = H^{-1} = \mathrm{diag}(1, 1/10) divides each direction by its own curvature, so every direction behaves like curvature 1: the valley becomes a perfectly round bowl, \kappa = 1. With \gamma = 1:

One step. Not “converges quickly”: lands exactly on the minimum in one step.

  geom_contour(aes(z = f), bins = 20, colour = "grey70") +

  geom_point(data = both_pre, aes(colour = method), size = 0.9) +

            (path_pre, "#009E73", "preconditioned, gamma = 1")]

x1, x2, f_grid = contour_data(f_ill, (-10, 3), (-4, 4))
fig, ax = plt.subplots()

for p, colour, label in both_pre:
    ax.plot(p["x1"], p["x2"], color=colour, linewidth=0.8, label=label)
    ax.scatter(p["x1"], p["x2"], color=colour, s=8)
ax.legend()
plt.show()










Taking P = (\nabla^2 f)^{-1}, recomputed at every iterate, with \gamma = 1, has a name: Newton’s method. On a quadratic it finishes in one step; near the minimum of a smooth function it converges quadratically (the number of correct digits roughly doubles per iteration). So why isn’t Newton the end of the chapter?

Cost. In d dimensions the Hessian has d^2 entries, and applying its inverse means solving a d \times d linear system: O(d^3) per step. For a neural network with d = 10^6 parameters, the Hessian alone would need terabytes of memory.
Fragility. Away from the minimum the Hessian need not be positive definite, and then -H^{-1}\nabla f may not even point downhill. Making Newton robust takes real engineering.

Cheap compromises are everywhere in statistics and machine learning: use only the diagonal of the Hessian (exactly our P above: for axis-aligned problems it is the whole story, and in general it is a decent approximation); or simply standardise your covariates, which is preconditioning by a diagonal matrix before the algorithm even starts. If you remember one practical trick from this section: rescale your variables before optimising. Exercise 5.3 shows what happens if you don’t.


5.2.2 BFGS: learning the Hessian as you go
Newton’s method needs second derivatives we cannot afford. But here is the clever observation: the gradients we are already computing contain second-order information. By Taylor expansion, for nearby iterates,

\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}) - \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_k)
\;\approx\;
H \, (\mathbf{x}_{k+1} - \mathbf{x}_k),

so each step tells us how the gradient changed when we moved in one particular direction: one slice of the Hessian, for free. Quasi-Newton methods maintain a running approximation B_k \approx H^{-1} and require it to explain the most recent step exactly, the secant condition:

B_{k+1} \, \underbrace{\big(\nabla f_{k+1} - \nabla f_k\big)}_{\mathbf{y}_k}
= \underbrace{\mathbf{x}_{k+1} - \mathbf{x}_k}_{\mathbf{s}_k}.

BFGS (Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno, 1970: four people found it independently in the same year) updates B_k by the smallest symmetric modification that satisfies the secant condition, a rank-two update: cheap matrix–vector algebra, no matrix inversion, and B_k stays positive definite so the step -B_k \nabla f_k always points downhill (provided each step actually observes positive curvature, \mathbf{y}_k^\top \mathbf{s}_k > 0: the line search inside optim() and minimize() sees to this). For the curious, the update is

B_{k+1} = \big(I - \rho_k \mathbf{s}_k \mathbf{y}_k^\top\big) B_k
          \big(I - \rho_k \mathbf{y}_k \mathbf{s}_k^\top\big)
          + \rho_k \mathbf{s}_k \mathbf{s}_k^\top,
\qquad \rho_k = \frac{1}{\mathbf{y}_k^\top \mathbf{s}_k},

and we will not derive it. The point to retain is the idea: start with B_0 = I (plain gradient descent), and let each observed gradient difference teach the algorithm a bit more of the local geometry. After a handful of steps BFGS is taking nearly Newton-quality steps while having only ever evaluated f and \nabla f.
Algorithm 5.4 collects the whole loop in one place.






Algorithm 5.4: BFGS



Input: objective f, gradient \nabla f, start point \mathbf{x}_0, tolerance \varepsilon > 0 (in practice also an iteration cap, as in optim() and minimize()).
Output: the final iterate, an approximate minimiser.

initialise B_0 \leftarrow I, so the first step is a plain gradient step
for k = 0, 1, 2, \dots until \|\nabla f_k\| \le \varepsilon:

step to \mathbf{x}_{k+1} \leftarrow \mathbf{x}_k - \gamma_k \, B_k \nabla f_k, with the step length \gamma_k chosen by a line search
record the step \mathbf{s}_k = \mathbf{x}_{k+1} - \mathbf{x}_k and the gradient difference \mathbf{y}_k = \nabla f_{k+1} - \nabla f_k
update B_k to B_{k+1} by the rank-two formula above: the smallest symmetric modification of B_k satisfying the secant condition B_{k+1} \mathbf{y}_k = \mathbf{s}_k (B_{k+1} stays positive definite because the line search ensures \mathbf{y}_k^\top \mathbf{s}_k > 0)

return the final iterate \mathbf{x}_k

Here \nabla f_k is short for \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_k), and B_k \approx H^{-1} throughout: this B is the traditional quasi-Newton symbol for the inverse-Hessian approximation, nothing to do with the mini-batches B_t of Algorithm 5.2.


You will never implement BFGS yourself, because both languages ship it (R as optim(), Python inside scipy.optimize.minimize()):


R
optim(par, fn, gr, method = "BFGS")


Python
sp.optimize.minimize(fun, x0, jac=grad, method="BFGS")


with par/x0 the starting point, fn/fun the function to minimise and gr/jac its gradient. Note that, unlike our grad_descent(), the built-in optimisers genuinely need the objective as well as the gradient: the line search inside BFGS evaluates fn to decide how far to step. The pieces we have been passing around all chapter slot straight in (this is why we wrote everything functional-style). Time to return to the logistic regression of Section 5.1.2 and retire our hand-tuned step sizes:


R

fit_bfgs <- optim(par = c(0, 0), fn = nll, gr = nll_grad, method = "BFGS")
fit_bfgs$par          # estimated coefficients

fit_bfgs = sp.optimize.minimize(nll, x0=np.zeros(2), jac=nll_grad, method="BFGS")
fit_bfgs.x            # estimated coefficients

array([-0.63803659,  1.89158111])

Note for Python: the report fields differ in name and convention: $par, $value, $counts and $convergence become .x, .fun, .nfev/.njev and .success. And R signals success with convergence == 0, scipy with success == True. Always check it, whatever it is called.
About a dozen gradient evaluations in either run (each language on its own draw of the data). Let us line it up against our own algorithms, and against a reference fit: glm(), R’s official logistic regression fitter, on the left; on the right, since Python has no built-in glm() (the usual tools live in the statsmodels package), BFGS rerun with a very strict tolerance, measuring cost in observation-gradients touched, as in Section 5.1.3:

# our SGD, with a hand-tuned decay schedule
set.seed(3)
path_sgd_nll <- sgd(nll_grad_i, c(0, 0), gamma = \(t) 10 / (20 + t),
                    n_steps = 4000, n_data = n_log)

# the reference fit
fit_glm <- glm(y_log ~ X_log - 1, family = binomial)

results <- data.frame(
  method = c("glm()", "optim BFGS", "GD (200 steps)", "SGD (4000 steps)"),
  nll = c(nll(coef(fit_glm)), fit_bfgs$value,

)

3        SGD (4000 steps)  0.452686         4,000




Read the table slowly: it summarises the whole chapter. (The two columns fit two different draws of the data, so the loss values differ between languages: the pattern is the same.)

BFGS matches the reference fit (glm() in R) to six decimals at the cost of a few thousand observation-gradients, with no tuning at all: no \gamma, no schedule, no \beta. The curvature information it accumulates replaces all the knobs we spent this chapter turning by hand.
GD gets there too, but only after we hand-tuned \gamma, and at over fifteen times the cost. On an ill-conditioned problem (Exercise 5.3) the gap grows by orders of magnitude.
SGD is nearly as accurate here at a fraction of the cost, and its cost would be unchanged if n were 10^8, which is the regime it is built for.

Two closing remarks on optim() and minimize(). For problems with many parameters there is method = "L-BFGS-B" (same name in both), a low-memory variant that stores only the last few (\mathbf{s}_k, \mathbf{y}_k) pairs instead of the full d \times d matrix (and accepts box constraints on the parameters). And practically: optim() with BFGS is what you reach for when fitting a model by maximum likelihood in R (minimize() in Python): countless packages in both languages are, under the hood, exactly optim(par, nll, gr, method = "BFGS") or its minimize() twin wearing a nice interface.






Exercise 5.3: optim / minimize in the wild



Fit a logistic regression predicting a car’s transmission type from its horsepower and weight, using the built-in mtcars data (am is 1 for manual; in Python the same data frame ships with plotnine):


R

X_cars <- cbind(1, mtcars$hp, mtcars$wt)
y_cars <- mtcars$am
n_cars <- nrow(mtcars)

nll_cars <- \(b) {
  eta <- as.vector(X_cars %*% b)
  mean(log(1 + exp(eta)) - y_cars * eta)
}
nll_cars_grad <- \(b) {
  p <- 1 / (1 + exp(-as.vector(X_cars %*% b)))
  as.vector(t(X_cars) %*% (p - y_cars)) / n_cars
}



Python

from plotnine.data import mtcars

X_cars = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(mtcars)), mtcars["hp"], mtcars["wt"]])
y_cars = mtcars["am"].to_numpy()
n_cars = len(mtcars)

def nll_cars(b):
    eta = X_cars @ b
    return np.mean(np.log(1 + np.exp(eta)) - y_cars * eta)

def nll_cars_grad(b):
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X_cars @ b)))
    return X_cars.T @ (p - y_cars) / n_cars




Fit with optim(c(0, 0, 0), nll_cars, nll_cars_grad, method = "BFGS") and compare the NLL at the optimum with glm(am ~ hp + wt, data = mtcars, family = binomial) (compute nll_cars(coef(...))). Check $convergence: if it is not 0, look up what that means in ?optim and fix it via the control argument.

5.3 Where you will see all this again
This chapter is a gateway. The same handful of ideas reappears, barely disguised, all over statistics and machine learning:

Maximum likelihood, everywhere. Almost every model you will fit from now on is fitted by numerically minimising a negative log-likelihood. Sometimes the optimiser is visible (optim() or minimize() in a package’s source code), sometimes hidden (R’s glm() uses iteratively reweighted least squares, a Newton variant), but it is always there, and now you know what its knobs mean and what its failure modes look like. When a model “fails to converge”, you have seen the picture: a too-large step diverging, or an ill-conditioned likelihood crawling.
Neural networks. Training a network is minimising an average loss over millions of observations and millions of parameters: mini-batch SGD is the core engine. However, as the geometry of the loss landscape is often ill-conditioned in those ML models, we tend to find that a separate class of gradient descent algorithms, called momentum based SGD, which include Adam. In short, these accelerate convergence by using a moving average of past gradients to smooth out the zig-zagging and help navigate the loss landscape more effectively.

Sampling algorithms. When you meet Markov chain Monte Carlo in weeks 8–10 of this module, you will find the same geometry problem in a new costume: a sampler exploring an elongated, ill-conditioned posterior zig-zags just like gradient descent did.
